title: Crystallisation
calcLabel: Read the solubility and yield guide
ends: Your crystals will filter like sand.

steps.q: 100 kg dissolved in 300 kg solvent, cooled to 5 °C, where solubility is 10 g per 100 g. Best yield?
steps.title: Yield from solubility
steps.summary: At 5 °C the solvent holds 10 g of product per 100 g, so 300 kg of solvent keeps 30 kg dissolved in the mother liquor. The maximum crystallised is 100 − 30 = 70 kg, a 70 % yield. Less solvent, a lower final temperature or an anti-solvent raise it; washing and handling losses bring the real yield a little lower.

steps.q: You crash-cool a batch fast. The crystals come out very fine and filter badly. Why?
steps.title: Crash cooling
steps.summary: Supersaturation, the excess of dissolved product over its solubility, drives crystallisation. Slow cooling keeps supersaturation low so existing crystals grow. Crash cooling drives supersaturation high, and the batch forms huge numbers of new nuclei instead, giving fine crystals that filter slowly and hold more mother liquor. Cool slowly, especially at the start.

draw: cool slowly, esp. at the start

steps.title: Seeding
steps.summary: Without seed, crystals nucleate at random, often late and suddenly. Seed crystals give dissolved product a surface to grow on at low supersaturation, so crystal form and size repeat batch after batch. Seed with the correct polymorph, as a slurry, at the right temperature.

draw: same form, same size, each batch

steps.q: On the solubility chart, where should you add the seed?
steps.title: Metastable zone
steps.summary: Below the solubility curve the solution is unsaturated and seed dissolves. Between the solubility curve and the metastable limit it is supersaturated but does not nucleate on its own. Add seed just inside this metastable zone, close to the solubility curve, so the seeds grow with little new nucleation, then cool slowly enough to stay in the zone.

draw: then cool slowly, stay in the zone

steps.q: On cooling, the product separates as an oily layer instead of crystals. Best first fix?
steps.title: Oiling out
steps.summary: Oiling out is the product separating as a liquid instead of crystals, often caused by high supersaturation, impurities or a low melting point. The oil traps impurities and sets into sticky lumps. Seed earlier at lower supersaturation and cool more slowly so crystals form first; if needed, change the solvent ratio or crystallisation temperature.

steps.q: Same compound, two different crystal forms (polymorphs). Why does it matter for a drug?
steps.title: Polymorphs
steps.summary: Polymorphs are crystal forms of the same molecule with different packing. They can differ in solubility, dissolution rate and stability, which changes how a drug behaves, so the approved form is part of the specification and the wrong form fails the batch. The form is controlled through solvent, temperature, cooling rate and seeding with the correct polymorph.

draw: the form is in the spec

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: crystallisation, where your product decides what shape it wants to be. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the solubility and yield guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. 100 kg dissolved in 300 kg solvent, cooled to 5 °C, where solubility is 10 g per 100 g. Best yield?

q1-r0.text: 90? You forgot how much stays dissolved in 300 kilos.

q1-r2.text: 100? Some always stays in the mother liquor.

q1-r3.text: 30 is what's lost, not what you get.

q1-b0.text: At 5 degrees, 100 grams of solvent can hold 10 grams of product.

q1-b1.text: 300 kilograms of solvent hold 30 kilograms. That stays in the mother liquor.

q1-b2.text: 100 minus 30 leaves 70 kilograms of crystals. 70 percent is the most you can get.

q1-b3.text: Less solvent, a colder end, or an anti-solvent all push it up. Real yield is a little lower, after washing and handling.

q2.text: Question 2. You crash-cool a batch fast. The crystals come out very fine and filter badly. Why?

q2-r0.text: Nothing evaporated. It's about how fast you cooled.

q2-r1.text: Yes! Millions of new crystals, none of them big.

q2-r2.text: Agitation matters, but this is about cooling too fast.

q2-r3.text: Fine crystals aren't decomposed. Just tiny.

q2-b0.text: Supersaturation is the driving force: how much more is dissolved than the solubility allows.

q2-b1.text: Cool slowly, and you stay just above the curve. Existing crystals grow.

q2-b2.text: Crash-cool, and supersaturation shoots up. The batch makes millions of new tiny crystals instead.

q2-b3.text: Fine crystals pack tight, filter slowly and hold more mother liquor. Cool slowly, at least at the start.

q3.text: Question 3. Why add seed crystals to a crystallisation?

q3-r0.text: Seeds don't change solubility. They give crystals a place to grow.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Growth on your terms, not random nucleation.

q3-r2.text: Seeds don't cool anything. The jacket does.

q3-r3.text: A percent or so of seed barely moves the yield.

q3-b0.text: Without seed, crystals appear at random, often late and all at once.

q3-b1.text: Seed gives the dissolved product a surface to grow on, at low supersaturation.

q3-b2.text: You get the same crystal form and size, batch after batch.

q3-b3.text: Use the right polymorph as seed, add it as a slurry, and add it at the right temperature.

q4.text: Question 4. On the solubility chart, where should you add the seed?

q4-r0.text: Undersaturated? Your seed will just dissolve.

q4-r1.text: Correct! Slightly supersaturated, before it nucleates on its own.

q4-r2.text: Too late. It's already nucleating by itself.

q4-r3.text: After filtration? That's not seeding, that's garnish.

q4-b0.text: Below the solubility curve the solution is unsaturated: seed dissolves.

q4-b1.text: Just above it is the metastable zone. Supersaturated, but it won't nucleate on its own yet.

q4-b2.text: Seed in that zone, close to the solubility curve. Seeds grow, and few new crystals form.

q4-b3.text: Then cool slowly enough to stay inside the zone until the end.

q5.text: Question 5. On cooling, the product separates as an oily layer instead of crystals. Best first fix?

q5-r0.text: Faster cooling pushes supersaturation higher. That's what makes oil.

q5-r1.text: Yes! Get crystals growing before the oil can form.

q5-r2.text: Stopping the agitator just lets the oil settle.

q5-r3.text: Faster anti-solvent means higher supersaturation. More oil, not less.

q5-b0.text: Oiling out happens when the product comes out as a liquid. High supersaturation, impurities or a low melting point can cause it.

q5-b1.text: The oil traps impurities. When it finally sets, you get sticky lumps, not clean crystals.

q5-b2.text: Seed earlier, at lower supersaturation, and cool slower, so crystals form before the oil can.

q5-b3.text: If that's not enough, change the solvent ratio or crystallise at a different temperature.

q6.text: Question 6. Same compound, two different crystal forms (polymorphs). Why does it matter for a drug?

q6-r0.text: Same molecule, different packing. The patient can tell the difference.

q6-r1.text: Correct! And so can stability, and how the drug works in the body.

q6-r2.text: Colour is the least of it.

q6-r3.text: Price is the least of it. A different form can change how much drug the patient absorbs.

q6-b0.text: Polymorphs are the same molecule, packed in a different crystal arrangement.

q6-b1.text: Different packing can mean different solubility, dissolution rate and stability. That changes how the drug behaves.

q6-b2.text: The approved form is in the specification. Making the wrong one is a failed batch.

q6-b3.text: Control it with the solvent, temperature, cooling rate and the right seed. Read the solubility and yield guide on pharmacheme dot in.
